interactions.label: A farmer presents with high fever, muscle pain, and red eyes after wading throug

params.question: A farmer presents with high fever, muscle pain, and red eyes after wading through flooded rice fields. Three other farmers from his village were recently hospitalised with similar symptoms. Which feature of this history most strongly points to a zoonotic aetiology?

answers.text: Multiple people from the same village are affected simultaneously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Clustering suggests a common source, but person-to-person outbreaks can also produce village-level clusters. It does not by itself indicate an animal reservoir.

answers.text: The patient's occupation involved exposure to water contaminated with animal urine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The hallmark of a zoonotic infection is transmission from animals to humans. Occupational exposure to flood water contaminated with rat or cattle urine is the classic route for leptospirosis — the animal reservoir is the key link.

answers.text: The presentation includes conjunctival suffusion and myalgia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These clinical signs raise suspicion for several febrile illnesses but do not by themselves indicate animal-to-human transmission, which is what defines a zoonosis.

answers.text: The illness occurred during the monsoon season in a coastal state

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Monsoon seasonality provides context for outbreaks but does not distinguish zoonotic from non-zoonotic causes, since many infectious diseases peak during the monsoon.

overallFeedback.feedback: The defining feature of a zoonosis is its animal-to-human transmission route. In this case, the farmer's contact with flood water contaminated by animal urine directly links the illness to a vertebrate animal reservoir — making occupational exposure the strongest indicator of zoonotic aetiology.

Exactly right. Zoonotic infections are defined by their animal-to-human transmission, and recognising the occupational exposure to animal-contaminated water is the crucial epidemiological clue in this case.

interactions.label: A sewer worker presents during monsoon season with high fever, jaundice, and acu

params.question: A sewer worker presents during monsoon season with high fever, jaundice, and acute kidney injury — the classic triad of Weil's disease. Which diagnostic test is considered the gold standard for confirming leptospirosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Blood culture on EMJH medium can isolate Leptospira in the first week of illness, but growth takes weeks and it is not considered the gold standard for confirmation.
Dark-field microscopy can visualise live spirochaetes, but it is prone to artefacts and false positives, making it unreliable as a confirmatory test.
Correct! MAT is the gold standard serological test for leptospirosis. It detects antibodies against specific Leptospira serovars and provides definitive confirmation of the diagnosis.
The IgM rapid test is useful for early point-of-care diagnosis from around day five of illness, but it is a screening tool, not the reference standard for confirmation.

overallFeedback.feedback: The microscopic agglutination test (MAT) is the gold standard for leptospirosis. While blood culture and IgM rapid tests are useful at different stages of illness, MAT provides the definitive serological confirmation.
Well done! MAT remains the reference standard for confirming leptospirosis, testing the patient's serum against panels of live Leptospira serovars to identify the infecting serogroup.

params.question: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4 count of 80 cells/μL presents with subacute headache, neck stiffness, and low-grade fever. CSF India ink preparation shows round organisms with a clear halo. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this infection?

answers.text: Reactivation of dormant Toxoplasma gondii cysts in the basal ganglia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Toxoplasma encephalitis presents with ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia on MRI, not meningitis with India ink-positive CSF. It involves parasite reactivation, but the clinical and laboratory picture here points elsewhere.

answers.text: Inhalation of a yeast from pigeon droppings, with haematogenous dissemination to the meninges

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Cryptococcus neoformans is a yeast linked to pigeon droppings. It enters through inhalation, disseminates haematogenously, and causes subacute meningitis at CD4 <100. India ink staining reveals the polysaccharide capsule as a clear halo — this finding is virtually diagnostic.

answers.text: Oropharyngeal colonisation by Candida albicans spreading to the central nervous system

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Candida causes oral thrush and oesophageal disease in immunocompromised patients, but CNS involvement is uncommon and it does not produce the characteristic India ink capsular halo described here.

answers.text: Reactivation of latent cytomegalovirus in the retinal vasculature

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CMV predominantly causes retinitis at CD4 <100, producing the characteristic 'pizza-pie' fundoscopic appearance. It does not typically present as subacute meningitis with India ink-positive CSF.

overallFeedback.feedback: The combination of subacute meningitis at CD4 <100 and India ink showing organisms with a clear capsular halo points to Cryptococcus neoformans — a yeast acquired by inhalation from pigeon droppings that disseminates to the meninges in severely immunocompromised patients.
Excellent. Cryptococcal meningitis from inhaled pigeon-associated yeast is a classic opportunistic infection at CD4 <100, and the India ink capsular halo is its signature diagnostic finding.

interactions.label: Hepatitis C virus causes hepatocellular carcinoma by integrating its DNA into th

params.question: Hepatitis C virus causes hepatocellular carcinoma by integrating its DNA into the host genome, similar to the mechanism used by Hepatitis B virus.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. HCV is an RNA virus that has no DNA stage at all, so it cannot integrate into the host genome the way HBV does. Instead, HCV causes hepatocellular carcinoma through chronic inflammation and viral protein-mediated interference with p53 — a fundamentally different mechanism from HBV's DNA integration.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well done. HCV is an RNA virus with no DNA stage — it cannot integrate into the host genome. Unlike HBV, which integrates its DNA and uses the HBx protein to activate oncogenes, HCV drives liver cancer through chronic inflammation and viral proteins that interfere with p53.

interactions.label: Which national health programme in India is responsible for the control of malar

params.question: Which national health programme in India is responsible for the control of malaria, dengue, chikungunya, kala-azar, and Japanese encephalitis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ni-kshay focuses specifically on tuberculosis, using DOTS therapy and GeneXpert testing, with a target of TB elimination by 2025 — ahead of the global 2030 target.
NACP is dedicated to HIV/AIDS control, providing free antiretroviral therapy, counselling and testing centres, and prevention of parent-to-child transmission.

Correct! The NVBDCP handles all major vector-borne diseases in India — malaria, dengue, chikungunya, lymphatic filariasis, kala-azar, and Japanese encephalitis — through integrated vector control, diagnosis, and treatment strategies.
IDSP coordinates surveillance of emerging infections across all states and union territories, but it is a surveillance and reporting system, not a disease-specific control programme.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct answer is the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP). It covers malaria, dengue, chikungunya, filariasis, kala-azar, and Japanese encephalitis under a single umbrella programme with integrated vector control.
That's right. The NVBDCP is India's comprehensive programme for all vector-borne diseases, combining vector control with diagnostic and treatment strategies across six major diseases.
